subsection: 7. Economic growth and social tensions: industrialisation in Germany and the Krupp family, 1871–1914

notes.h: The starting point: Britain, the new Reich and a customs union
notes.b: To see how fast Germany industrialised, you need to know where it started in 1871. Britain was still ahead, and Germany had only just become one state.
points: The first industrial revolution (based on coal, iron, textiles and steam power) began in Britain, which was still the leading industrial power in 1871. Germany was catching up, which is why its later growth looks so dramatic.

The Reich was proclaimed in January 1871 as a federation of states dominated by Prussia. The Reichstag was elected by universal male suffrage, but the Chancellor answered to the Kaiser, not to the Reichstag.

Prussia kept its own three-class franchise (voters grouped by the taxes they paid, so the rich counted for more) until 1918. This matters later because it shut workers out of power in the largest state.

The Zollverein (a customs union led by Prussia, founded in 1834, which Austria did not join) had already removed most customs barriers between the German states, so unification built on an existing common market.
By the Treaty of Frankfurt (1871) France gave Alsace and part of Lorraine to Germany and paid an indemnity of 5 billion francs. Both the territory and the money helped German industry.
notes.tip: In a higher essay on the impact of industrialisation, put a clear judgement in your first sentence, then explain why each cause mattered rather than listing them. Britain in 1871 and the Zollverein are the starting point for your causes.

notes.h: Why Germany industrialised fast after 1871: resources, market and railways
notes.b: Germany had the raw materials, the people and the transport that heavy industry needs. Unification then turned many small markets into one large one.
points: Germany's population grew from about 41 million in 1871 to about 65 million in 1910 and about 67 million in 1914, which supplied both workers for the factories and a large home market to buy their goods.

Coal and iron were the base of heavy industry. The Ruhr (in Westphalia) was the heart of it, with more coal in the Saar and Upper Silesia, and iron ore (called minette) in Lorraine, the part annexed from France in 1871.

Unification created a single market. The mark became the one currency in 1873, the Reichsbank (the central bank) was founded in 1875 and opened in 1876, and commercial law was made common, so firms no longer faced different rules in each state.

Railways grew from about 20,000 km around 1870 to more than 60,000 km by 1913, linking the Ruhr to cities and ports. They were also a huge market in their own right, because tracks and engines used vast amounts of coal and steel.
From 1879 Prussia bought out most private railway companies, so the state owned most of the network.
The French indemnity gave the new Reich a financial boost, and the early 1870s boom (the Gründerzeit, 'founding years') followed. It ended in the stock market crash of 1873.
After the crash, prices and profits stayed depressed for much of the period to the mid-1890s. This long depression pushed firms towards cartels and the state towards tariffs.
notes.tip: Examiners reward explaining why each cause mattered, not listing them. For railways, say they linked the Ruhr to ports and also created demand for coal and steel.

notes.h: Why Germany industrialised fast after 1871: banks, education, cartels and the state
notes.b: Resources alone do not build an industry. German firms also had access to long-term money, trained engineers, organised markets and a supportive state, and as a late starter they could build new.
points: Universal banks, such as Deutsche Bank (founded 1870) and Dresdner Bank (1872), lent to industry for long periods and sat on company boards. This let firms raise the capital that heavy investment in plant needed.

Technische Hochschulen (technical universities), found in cities such as Berlin (Charlottenburg), Munich and Aachen, and technical schools trained engineers and chemists. Chemical and electrical firms ran their own research laboratories, so science and industry were closely linked.

A cartel is an agreement among firms to fix prices, share markets or limit output. They spread after the 1873 crash and long depression because firms wanted to protect profits, and there were several hundred by the early 1900s.
Examples of cartels include the Rhenish-Westphalian Coal Syndicate (1893), which controlled most Ruhr coal, and the Steel Works Association (Stahlwerksverband, 1904).
Large combined firms also grew, with mines, ironworks and engineering under one owner. August Thyssen built such a concern in the Ruhr, covering coal, iron and steel.
The state helped industry. The protective tariff of 1879 taxed imported iron, steel and grain, and the army, navy and state railways were large customers for steel and equipment.
Germany also gained from a late start. Its firms built new plant with the latest technology, instead of patching up older works as British firms often had to.
notes.tip: Include cartels and the depression link: examiners look for why cartels spread. Name the Coal Syndicate and the Steel Works Association as evidence.

notes.h: The scale of German growth by 1914
notes.b: The result of these causes was growth that alarmed Germany's rivals. In steel, chemicals and electricals Germany overtook Britain, though not in every industry.
points: Hard coal output rose from about 30 million tonnes in 1871 to about 190 million tonnes in 1913, about a six-fold increase. Britain, however, still mined more coal than Germany in 1913.

In 1913 Germany produced about 17 million tonnes of steel, against about 8 million for Britain, so more than twice as much. Remember that Germany overtook Britain in steel, chemicals and electricals, not in coal.
By 1914 Germany was the second industrial power in the world after the USA. On most estimates its share of world manufacturing roughly matched or slightly exceeded Britain's by 1913.

Exports of machinery, chemicals and electrical goods competed with British goods across the world. Britain's Merchandise Marks Act (1887) required goods to show where they were made, and E. E. Williams's book 'Made in Germany' (1896) warned of German competition.

The Hamburg-America Line (HAPAG, led by Albert Ballin) and North German Lloyd of Bremen carried this trade. HAPAG was the world's largest shipping company by 1914, and Germany's merchant fleet was second only to Britain's.
German emigration, mostly to the USA, peaked in the 1880s and fell steeply after the early 1890s. This is because industry was by then creating jobs at home.
notes.tip: Be exact about what Germany overtook. Say steel, chemicals and electricals, and note that Britain still mined more coal in 1913; giving this precision protects you from a common error.

notes.h: The second industrial revolution: steel, chemicals and electricals
notes.b: From about the 1880s new industries based on steel, chemicals and electricity grew faster than the older coal and textiles. This is called the second industrial revolution, and Germany was often the leader.
points: Steel: the basic (Thomas-Gilchrist) process was invented by two Britons, Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and Percy Gilchrist, in 1878-79. It made the phosphoric iron ore of Lorraine usable for steel, and German steelmakers took up the licence quickly, so steel output soared in the Ruhr.
Chemicals: BASF (Ludwigshafen, 1865), Bayer (1863) and Hoechst (1863) led the world. By 1914 Germany made the great majority of the world's synthetic dyes, and Bayer marketed aspirin from 1899.
Fritz Haber synthesised ammonia from nitrogen in 1909, and Carl Bosch scaled the process up at BASF, with the first plant at Oppau in 1913. Before 1914 it was used for artificial fertilisers.

Electricals: Werner von Siemens and Johann Georg Halske founded Siemens & Halske in Berlin in 1847, at first making telegraphs. Siemens built a dynamo (a machine that generates electricity) in 1866-67.
Siemens showed an electric railway at the Berlin trade exhibition in 1879 and ran an electric tram at Lichterfelde, Berlin, in 1881.

Emil Rathenau founded the Deutsche Edison-Gesellschaft in 1883, renamed AEG (Allgemeine Elektricitäts-Gesellschaft) in 1887. Electric lighting, trams and power stations spread in cities from the 1880s and 1890s, and by 1914 Siemens and AEG dominated the industry.
Engines and motor cars: Karl Benz and Gottlieb Daimler built motor cars in the 1880s, and Rudolf Diesel developed the diesel engine in the 1890s.
notes.tip: For a Higher essay on industry in Europe, have German examples ready: steel, Siemens and AEG, the chemical firms and Krupp. Do not say the process of 1878-79 was German, because it was British and German firms licensed it.

notes.h: Key personality: the Krupp family - Alfred Krupp
notes.b: The Krupp works at Essen grew from a small steel workshop into one of the largest industrial enterprises in Europe, and its name became linked with German arms and industry. Alfred Krupp, the Cannon King, made it so.
points: Friedrich Krupp founded a cast steel works at Essen in 1811 and died in 1826. His son Alfred Krupp (1812-87) then took charge aged 14, when the firm was small and in debt.
At the Great Exhibition in London in 1851 Alfred showed a flawless cast steel ingot of about 2 tons, which won him international attention. He also showed a steel cannon.

He developed seamless steel railway wheel tyres, patented in the early 1850s. Their three interlocking rings became the firm's trademark. He took up the Bessemer process in the early 1860s and made steel for railways.

Alfred moved into artillery. Prussia adopted his breech-loading steel guns (loaded from the rear) in the 1860s, and in 1870-71 they outranged and outperformed French bronze muzzle-loaders in the war against France.
He sold guns to many states, including Russia and the Ottoman Empire, which earned him the nickname 'the Cannon King' (Kanonenkönig).
Welfare: from the 1860s Alfred built housing estates (colonies) for workers and provided sickness and pension funds, schools, shops (including a co-operative store) and a hospital.

Control: in 1877 he issued an appeal urging his workers to stay out of politics, and known socialists were dismissed. Historians call this paternalism, meaning care that is given in return for obedience.
He completed Villa Hügel, the family house above the Ruhr, in 1873. By his death in July 1887 the works employed about 20,000 workers.
notes.tip: A paragraph on the Krupps needs accurate, dated statements across the generations. Cover the 1811 founding, Alfred taking over young, the 1851 ingot, railway tyres, guns and Prussia's wars, and the Cannon King, with welfare shown as paternalism.

notes.h: Key personality: the Krupp family - Friedrich Alfred Krupp
notes.b: Alfred's son Friedrich Alfred took the firm from guns for armies into armour and ships for the new German navy. Do not confuse him with the founder, Friedrich Krupp, who died in 1826.
points: Friedrich Alfred Krupp (1854-1902) headed the firm from 1887 to 1902.
In 1893 he bought the Gruson works at Magdeburg, which made armour plate. Krupp nickel-steel armour plate was widely used by navies, so the firm profited as fleets grew.
He took over the Germania shipyard at Kiel from 1896 (it was renamed Fried. Krupp Germaniawerft in 1902), which gave the firm shipbuilding. It later built U-boats there.
Wilhelm II was a personal friend and frequent visitor, and the fleet was a major customer. This shows how the firm and the state depended on each other.
In mid-November 1902 Vorwärts (the SPD newspaper) printed allegations about his private life on Capri. He died on 22 November 1902, officially of a stroke, though suicide was widely suspected.
Wilhelm II attended the funeral in Essen and then publicly attacked the SPD, which shows how closely the Kaiser, the firm and the political struggle with socialism were linked.
notes.tip: Do not say Friedrich Alfred bought the Germania yard in 1902. Say Krupp took it over from 1896. Keep the two Friedrichs and Alfred apart: the Cannon King is Alfred.

notes.h: Key personality: the Krupp family - Bertha and Gustav
notes.b: After 1902 the firm passed to a young heiress and her diplomat husband. Under them Krupp became the arms maker whose guns were used in the first months of the First World War.
points: Bertha Krupp (1886-1957) inherited the firm in 1902 aged 16. In 1903 it became a joint-stock company, Fried. Krupp AG, and Bertha held almost all the shares.

Gustav von Bohlen und Halbach (1870-1950), a Prussian diplomat, married Bertha in October 1906 with Wilhelm II present. The Kaiser allowed him the name Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach, so he was not born a Krupp. He ran the firm, chairing its supervisory board from 1909.

The Kornwalzer scandal (1913): the SPD deputy Karl Liebknecht exposed in the Reichstag that Krupp's Berlin agent had bribed War Ministry clerks for secret information. A trial followed in 1913, and the affair took its name from a code word used.

In August 1914 the 42 cm howitzer nicknamed 'Big Bertha' (Dicke Bertha), usually said to be named after Bertha Krupp, was used against the Belgian forts of Liège and Namur. Do not confuse it with the Paris Gun of 1918.
In the war the firm made guns, shells, armour and U-boats (built at Kiel). Its workforce passed 100,000, and many women worked in its shell shops.
notes.tip: Cover Bertha and Gustav, not just Alfred, or you lose marks. Name the 1913 bribery case as the Kornwalzer affair, with Liebknecht, and give Big Bertha in 1914 as evidence of Krupp's link to war.

notes.h: Key personality: the Krupp family - how they shaped events and how they are judged
notes.b: The Krupps both shaped German history and were shaped by it. Contemporaries and historians judged them very differently depending on their politics.
points: Shaped events: the Krupps armed Prussia and the Reich, and profited from unification, the naval race and war. Krupp was often described as the largest industrial firm in Europe before 1914.
Shaped by events: the firm also depended on state orders and on the Kaiser's favour, so its success was tied to Prussian and German power.
Contemporaries: to nationalists and the Kaiser, Krupp was a national symbol of German industrial and military strength.
To socialists, the Krupps were exploiters who profited from armaments and controlled their workers. Socialists attacked the firm for profiting from armaments.

To historians Krupp is the leading example of the link between heavy industry, the army and the state before 1914, which some call a military-industrial complex, and as the model of industrial paternalism.
The firm's later role under the Nazis falls outside this period.
notes.tip: Give both views: Krupp as an admired national symbol and as an arms profiteer who controlled its workers. For a question on technology, industry, prestige and war, use the Krupp guns and Big Bertha as evidence.

notes.h: Urbanisation and the growth of the working class
notes.b: Industry needed workers, and they came from the countryside. This created a large urban working class, with new problems and new political strength.
points: Millions moved from the countryside, especially from the agrarian east (the 'flight from the land'), to Berlin and the Ruhr, because industry offered work. Polish-speaking migrants to the Ruhr were nicknamed 'Ruhrpolen'.
About a third of Germans (about 36 per cent) lived in towns of 2,000 or more in 1871. By 1910 the figure was about 60 per cent.
Berlin grew from about 830,000 (under a million) in 1871 to about 2 million in 1910. Essen grew from about 50,000 to about 300,000, with suburbs absorbed, so Ruhr towns grew many times over.

Berlin's workers lived in Mietskasernen ('rental barracks'), large tenement blocks around courtyards. They were overcrowded, with poor sanitation and disease, though public health and city services improved from the 1890s.
Working conditions meant long hours, strict factory discipline and insecurity, and women and children worked too. Real wages rose slowly from the 1890s.
The Labour Protection Law of 1891 gave Sunday rest, a maximum 11-hour day for women and banned factory work for children under 13.
Strikes showed workers' strength. In May 1889 about 90,000 Ruhr miners struck and Wilhelm II received a delegation of miners. A second, larger Ruhr strike came in January-February 1905.

The working class was divided. Catholic workers were often loyal to the Centre Party and Christian unions, Polish workers faced pressure to become German (Germanisation), and skilled workers differed from unskilled.
notes.tip: Link urbanisation to its results in the exam: the cities created the working class from which the SPD and the unions drew support.

notes.h: The SPD: founding, programme and growth
notes.b: A large urban working class gave a party based on Marxism its chance. Marxism teaches that society is a class struggle between owners and workers, and aims at common ownership of industry. The SPD became Germany's Marxist party.
points: The General German Workers' Association was founded by Ferdinand Lassalle in 1863. The Social Democratic Workers' Party was founded at Eisenach in 1869 by August Bebel and Wilhelm Liebknecht.
They united at Gotha in May 1875 as the Socialist Workers' Party, which took the name SPD (Social Democratic Party) in 1890.
The Anti-Socialist Law (passed October 1878, lapsed 30 September 1890) banned socialist organisations and press. Socialists could still stand for the Reichstag, and their vote rose.

The Erfurt Programme (October 1891), drafted mainly by Karl Kautsky (theory) and Eduard Bernstein (demands), combined a Marxist analysis of capitalism with immediate demands such as democratic suffrage, the eight-hour day and social reforms.

Revisionism: Bernstein, in 'The Preconditions of Socialism' (1899), argued for gradual reform instead of revolution. The party congress at Dresden in 1903 condemned his ideas, but in practice the party acted as a reformist party.
In 1890 the SPD won about 1.4 million votes and 35 seats. In 1912 it won about 4.25 million votes (about a third of the total) and 110 of 397 seats, becoming the largest party in the Reichstag.
notes.tip: Keep the dates apart: Eisenach 1869, Gotha 1875, Erfurt 1891. Do not say the SPD was formed at Gotha under that name, because the party took the SPD name only in 1890.

notes.h: The SPD's limits, the unions and the socialist subculture
notes.b: Despite its votes the SPD could not win power, and employers and the state fought the labour movement. Yet the movement built a world of its own.
points: The SPD was strongest in the Reichstag, but the Chancellor was not answerable to the Reichstag, and the Bundesrat (the council of state governments) also limited it.

Constituencies had not changed since 1871, which favoured the countryside over the growing cities. The Prussian three-class franchise kept the SPD almost out of the Prussian parliament, and no SPD member was in government before 1918.
The Free Trade Unions (socialist) had about 2.5 million members in 1913, far more than the Christian (Catholic-led) unions and the liberal (Hirsch-Duncker) unions.
Employers replied with associations, lockouts and blacklists. The police and courts were also used against strikes.
The SPD built a socialist subculture of party newspapers, clubs, choirs, sports and education societies. This gave members a community, which helps explain why the party grew despite repression.
Critics called the SPD a 'state within a state', and its members were treated as outsiders (Reichsfeinde, 'enemies of the Reich'). Repression created martyrs and so kept loyalty strong.
notes.tip: To explain why the SPD grew despite repression and welfare, give the urban working class, the unions, the subculture and repression creating martyrs. Do not mix up the Reichstag (universal male suffrage) with the Prussian parliament (three-class franchise).

notes.h: Social tensions: Junkers, industrialists and workers
notes.b: Industrial growth changed the balance of power between landowners, factory owners and workers. Tariffs, which were taxes on imports, were the sharpest dispute.
points: The Junkers were landowning nobles of the Prussian lands east of the Elbe. They dominated the army officer corps, the Prussian civil service and the Prussian parliament, where three-class voting gave the rich more weight.
From the late 1870s cheap US and Russian grain threatened Junker profits. The tariff of 1879 protected grain and iron, creating the 'iron and rye' alliance of heavy industry and Junkers.

Caprivi (Chancellor 1890-94) lowered grain duties in trade treaties (1891-94). The Agrarian League (Bund der Landwirte), founded in 1893, campaigned against them. Bülow's tariff, passed in 1902 and in force in 1906, raised grain duties again.
Tariffs had losers. Dearer bread angered workers and consumers, and exporting and finished-goods industries and the left opposed high duties. 'Bread usury' was an SPD theme.

Sammlungspolitik (the 'policy of rallying together'), associated with Johannes von Miquel from 1897, aimed to unite landowners and industrialists behind the monarchy, the fleet and Weltpolitik (world policy), against the SPD.

Industrialists resented aristocratic privilege, but many copied the nobility with titles, estates and reserve-officer commissions. Hans-Ulrich Wehler (The German Empire 1871-1918) called this the 'feudalisation of the bourgeoisie' and saw it as part of a German 'special path' (Sonderweg).
David Blackbourn and Geoff Eley replied in 'The Peculiarities of German History' (1984) that the German middle class was confident and the Reich a modern society.

The middle classes also feared socialism, which led many to support nationalist pressure groups and the monarchy. Other tensions were the Kulturkampf against Catholics, and the position of Poles and the Alsace-Lorraine population.
notes.tip: For tensions, explain who was in conflict with whom and why. Say tariffs gave profit to Junkers but dearer food to workers, and name at least one historian with their view.

notes.h: The state's response: welfare and repression
notes.b: The state tried both to win workers over and to hold them down, a mix described as carrot and stick. Employers copied the carrot with welfare of their own.
points: Bismarck's social insurance created sickness insurance (1883), accident insurance (1884) and old age and invalidity insurance (1889). Its aim was to win workers from the SPD, a mix of welfare and repression known as 'carrot and stick'.

In 1890 Wilhelm II's 'new course' let the Anti-Socialist Law lapse. In February 1890 he issued decrees on workers' protection, and an international labour conference met in Berlin in March 1890. The Labour Protection Law followed in 1891.

The state then turned back to repression. The Subversion Bill (Umsturzvorlage, rejected 1895) and the Penitentiary Bill (Zuchthausvorlage, penalties for pressuring workers to strike, rejected 1899) both failed in the Reichstag. The Kaiser turned against the SPD because it kept winning votes.
Social insurance was consolidated in the Imperial Insurance Code (Reichsversicherungsordnung) of 1911.
Companies provided welfare too. Krupp's housing, schools and funds are the best-known example, and Siemens set up a pension fund in the 1870s. Employers wanted loyalty and no strikes.
Welfare did not stop the SPD vote from rising, because many workers were more loyal to their unions and party than to the state or firm.
No political reform followed economic change, and the Prussian three-class franchise survived to 1918.
notes.tip: Say why the state introduced welfare: to weaken the SPD. Then show its limits, because the SPD vote kept rising. Do not confuse the Anti-Socialist Law (passed) with the Subversion and Penitentiary Bills (rejected).

notes.h: Assessment: industrial success and social cost
notes.b: Judgement questions reward weighing achievement against limit, and contemporary views against later ones. The points below are set out in pairs.
points: Achievement: Germany became continental Europe's leading industrial economy and led in steel, chemicals and electricals.
Limit: growth was uneven, because agriculture and the east lagged, and the economy suffered boom and slump, as with the crash of 1873 and the long depression.
Achievement: Germany built the first national social insurance system, and real wages rose and emigration fell from the 1890s.
Limit: welfare was paternalist and paired with repression, the political system stayed closed to the largest party, and class, religious and regional tensions were unresolved in 1914.
Impact abroad: industrial power fed militarism, the arms industry and the naval race, and also trade rivalry with Britain.
Contemporary views: nationalists saw industrial power as proof of German greatness, while socialists saw exploitation.
Later views: historians debate whether Germany had a modern economy with an unreformed political system (Wehler) or was a normal modern society (Blackbourn and Eley).
notes.tip: Open an impact essay with a clear judgement, then link causes to results in society, politics and foreign policy, not just the economy. Name Krupp as admired national symbol and as arms profiteer.

keyTerms.definition: The expansion from the 1880s of industries based on steel, chemicals, electricity and the internal combustion engine, in which Germany led.
An agreement among firms in an industry to fix prices, share markets or limit output; common in German coal, steel and chemicals.
A German-style bank that lent to industry for the long term and took part in company management, such as Deutsche Bank.
The landowning nobility of eastern Prussia, who dominated the army and Prussian state and relied on tariffs to protect agriculture.
The German socialist party founded at Gotha in 1875; it became the largest party in the Reichstag in 1912.
The practice of employers, as at Krupp, providing housing, schools and benefits in return for loyalty and discipline.
The policy of rallying landowners and industrialists together behind the monarchy, the navy and tariffs against the left.
The protective tariff on grain and iron that linked heavy industry with the Junkers in an alliance of iron and rye.
